feature: A performance budget that measures the machine it is standing on
summary: The render speed checks used to compare against a flat number, with a second flat number for the build machine, so a slow build machine read as a slower app and stopped the v0.15.0 release twice. Each check now measures how fast the machine it is running on actually is and scales its limit to that, and a release never gates on a timing at all.
setup: Nothing to install or turn on. This is the test suite and the two build workflows. Run it from the repo root.

try.do: Run `Scripts/test.sh --no-parallel --filter RenderPerfTests` and read the `[perf] machine yardstick` lines: they say how fast this machine is against the one the numbers were recorded on.
Read a `[perf] budget:` line under it. It prints what was measured, what it was allowed, and the machine speed that decided the allowance.
Open https://github.com/dzearing/photonz/actions/runs/34717321829 and find the same lines in the Run tests step, to see the build machine describe itself as 2.74x and 3.45x slower.
Compare against the run an hour earlier, https://github.com/dzearing/photonz/actions/runs/34713295488, which failed the export check at 1439ms against a limit that had just been raised to 1400.
Run `PHOTONZ_PERF_GATE=report Scripts/test.sh --no-parallel --filter RenderPerfTests`. Every number still prints, nothing asserts. This is exactly what the release workflow now does.
Read the new section at the bottom of docs/progress/perf.md for the before and after margins on every budget.

evaluate: When a budget does fail, does the printed line tell you enough to know whether the app got slower or the machine was slow?
Is a release that never checks its own speed the right trade, given every commit in it already passed the check on the way to main?
The limits are now two and a half times a recorded number rather than seven to sixteen times it. Is that too tight for comfort, or still too loose to be interesting?
The recorded numbers are constants with a date in the file. Is hand-updating them when the development machine changes acceptable, or should that be automatic?
Is `[perf] budget:` on every run useful, or is it noise in a 5745-test log?
rough: No screenshot: this change has no on-screen surface at all. It lives in the test suite and two workflow files, so the evidence is log lines and CI runs, linked above.

The done task 'timing-budget-tests-pass-reliably-on-a-busy-machi' (2026-09-02) did not cover this, and could not have. It fixed CPU-bound checks by timing them on the thread's own CPU clock and asserting a ratio against a probe run back to back. PerfClock's own header says why that cannot reach here: it 'cannot see work handed to another thread or the GPU', and these renders are Core Image. Proof: ten CPU burners running flat out moved these numbers not at all, while running the same suite in parallel with everything else moved them by 30 to 40 percent.

The rulers under-read the machine a little. On the last CI run the composite subjects were 2.7x to 4.9x slower while the filter-graph ruler said 2.74x, and the export was 5.25x while its ruler said 3.45x. The two-and-a-half times tolerance absorbs that; the thinnest margins left are the 200 percent zoom tile at 1.8x and the export at 1.7x. Not a problem today, worth a look if either ever fails.

First attempt at the export ruler was wrong in exactly the way the task warned about. Reading 12 megapixels back from a trivial graph measured the runner at 3.4x while the real export was 8.2x, leaving six percent of headroom. Fixed by making the ruler produce a big picture rather than copy one. Caught only because the change was run on a real runner before being called done.

A budget whose recorded number is under about 16ms only catches regressions bigger than about 3.7x, because of the 8ms of absolute slack that keeps scheduler noise from deciding a 7ms measurement. That affects the interactive edits and the zoom tiles. It is still far better than the flat 100ms they had, which a 5x regression walked straight through.

The CI run is still red, for a different reason, now filed as 'A committed lock file stops every build on CI': queue/playtest.lock is tracked in git, so the build machine checks it out and Scripts/build-app.sh refuses to build. That would fail a release too, at the Build app step.
